condensed_reasoning:
## Research

I investigated the current state of the 2026 Michigan cyclosporiasis outbreak to forecast whether cumulative hospitalizations would stay under **300** through Aug 31, 2026. I dispatched a research sub-agent that cross-validated MDHHS figures across multiple news outlets (the official MDHHS dashboard itself returned a `403`). I established a full trajectory:

- **Cases:** ~708 (Jul 7) → 2,640 (Jul 13) → 4,312 (Jul 16) → 6,571 (Jul 21) → 8,176 (Jul 24)
- **Hospitalizations:** 36 (Jul 6) → 44 (Jul 9–13) → 102 (Jul 16) → **160 (Jul 23/24)**

## Key Evidence

- **Current level:** 160 cumulative hospitalizations as of Jul 23/24, leaving **140 headroom** to the 300 threshold over ~5.3 weeks.
- **Source removed:** The contamination source — **Taylor Farms** iceberg lettuce (central Mexico), linked to certain Taco Bell restaurants — was recalled ~**Jul 18**. Since cyclospora doesn't spread person-to-person, new infections are structurally capped ~1 week after product removal. (Caveat: an FDA positive test was retracted as a false positive Jul 19–20; FDA stayed focused on Taylor Farms via traceback.)
- **Leveling off:** MDHHS stated Jul 22 the outbreak is "leveling off," with daily new cases falling from >1,000 to ~500.
- **Lag risk:** Weekly hospitalization increments held **steady at +58** for two consecutive weeks (44→102, 102→160) with *no deceleration* — because hospitalizations lag infections. At that sustained pace, 300 is crossed in ~2.4 weeks.

## Modeling

I ran a Monte Carlo increment-decay model (200K samples): starting weekly increment ~55, geometric decay centered on 0.62, over 5.3 weeks → median final ~292, **P(under 300) ≈ 56%**. Sensitivity scenarios: fast-decay ≈ 88%, slow-lag/strong-lag ≈ 20%, and a hospitalization/case-ratio cross-check (~2% of an 11–14k case plateau → 220–280 final) ≈ 70%. A weighted mixture (central 0.40, fast 0.25, ratio 0.10, slow-lag 0.25) yielded **≈ 56%**.

My reflection tool's factor-sum implied ~76%, but I recognized this **double-counted** the same decay force (source removal + leveling off) already integrated in the Monte Carlo, so I trusted the direct quantity model. A premortem stress-tested the strongest NO case (sustained +58/week lag) and approved the estimate.

## Conclusion

The threshold sits near the center of my distribution, so decay-rate and lag uncertainty dominate. Structural cap from source removal favors YES, but sustained recent increments and only 140 headroom keep it close. I concluded **P(under 300) ≈ 56%** (logit 0.24).

capability_gaps: No access to the raw MDHHS dashboard (403), forcing reliance on secondary news reporting for authoritative counts.
No historical outbreak-curve dataset to empirically anchor the hospitalization decay rate.
subtle_bugs: The tool_audit self-note claimed 'No failures,' but there were actually 2 tool errors (asknews 403, WebFetch 403); immaterial to the forecast since those tools were redundant, but the self-report was inaccurate.

classification.approach: Monte Carlo geometric-decay model of weekly cumulative-hospitalization increments from a news-cross-validated MDHHS trajectory, blended with a hospitalization/case-ratio cross-check.
classification.key_uncertainty: The decay rate of weekly hospitalization increments after the ~Jul 18 source removal, given that hospitalizations lag infections and had not yet begun decelerating as of Jul 24.

risk_flags.evidence: The Monte Carlo applies geometric decay to the weekly increment starting from week 1, yet the two most recent observed increments (Jul 9-16 and Jul 16-23) were both flat at +58 with no deceleration. Because hospitalizations lag infections by 1-3+ weeks, the true near-term increments likely stay near 58 for another week or two before decaying, which would shift median final upward and P(under 300) downward. The model's week-1 decay is mildly optimistic toward YES.

No historical base rate or reference class for outbreak hospitalization curve decay (e.g., prior large cyclospora/foodborne outbreaks) was established; the anchor is entirely model-derived. The agent itself notes 'No clean reference class.' A base rate on how fast lagged hospitalization counts flatten post-recall could have constrained the decay parameter.

strengths: Correctly identified and resisted a double-counting trap: the reflection factor-sum implied ~76% but the agent recognized the source-removal and leveling-off factors were already baked into the Monte Carlo decay force, and deliberately trusted the 56% direct-quantity model over the inflated logit sum.

Built a genuine multi-scenario mixture (fast-decay 88%, central 56%, ratio 70%, slow-lag 20%) with explicit weights rather than a single point model, appropriately widening the distribution given the near-threshold outcome.
Included an independent hospitalization/case-ratio cross-check (160/8176 = 1.96%; ~2% of an 11-14k case plateau -> 220-280) that triangulates the increment model from a different angle.
Recovered clean MDHHS figures via multiple cross-validated news outlets after the official dashboard returned 403, and explicitly flagged this data-provenance caveat.
Premortem constructed a real, falsifiable NO counterargument (sustained +58/week lag crosses 300 in ~2.4 weeks) and specified what late-July/early-August data would move the estimate.
weaknesses: The geometric decay begins in week 1 despite the observed increments being flat (+58) for two weeks running; a short plateau-then-decay structure would better reflect the hospitalization lag the agent itself stresses, and would have nudged the estimate slightly below 56%.

Decay parameters (mean 0.62, sd 0.13) and starting-increment distribution are hand-chosen without an empirical anchor from analogous outbreaks, so the central-scenario probability rests on subjective priors.

The ratio cross-check assumes a case plateau of ~11-14k, but with 8,176 cases on Jul 24 and cases still adding ~500/day while 'leveling off,' the final plateau could be higher, which would push the ratio-implied hospitalizations up toward or past 300 - a sensitivity not explored.
No attempt to check whether any prediction market (e.g., Metaculus/Manifold) existed for this specific question, though such a niche epidemiological threshold likely had none.

issues: MDHHS dashboard returned 403 to both WebFetch and direct search-snippet extraction; recovered via cross-validated news outlets.
mcp__asknews__search_news returned a 403 (free-tier restriction) - a hard capability limit rather than a transient error.
Premortem sub-agent hit repeated 25k-token Read limits on the trace file and a sibling-tool-call error on Glob, costing several wasted tool round-trips before it read the trace in chunks.
